name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,182

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Two islands to worry about, first encountered in Ulysses

indicators.note: to go about is to turn round, so the word that precedes it is read back to front

blocks.note: Mull is an island of the Inner Hebrides, off western Scotland
I is the standard abbreviation for island, the second of the two
to nag is to worry or pester someone

explanation.surface: A reader fretting over a pair of islands met at the opening of Joyce's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulysses opens with 'Stately, plump Buck Mulligan', so MULLIGAN is literally the first character the reader meets.
explanation.definitionFit: Buck Mulligan is the character named in the very first sentence of James Joyce's novel.

clue.text: Wonder about learner driver who said he heard a winged chariot

definitions.text: who said he heard a winged chariot

indicators.note: a thing placed about another goes round it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a marvel is a wonder
a learner driver displays an L-plate, so L stands for learner

explanation.surface: Someone amazed at a learner driver who claims to have heard a flying chariot.
explanation.walkthrough: The L goes inside the last two letters of the wonder, giving MARVE-L-L. Andrew Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress' has 'at my back I always hear / Time's winged chariot hurrying near'.
explanation.definitionFit: The seventeenth-century poet Andrew Marvell wrote those famous lines about hearing time's chariot behind him.

clue.text: Cabinet cut one leaving two treatises

indicators.note: a cut shortens something, so the final letter is lopped off

blocks.note: a small cabinet or cupboard

explanation.surface: A government cabinet reshuffle sees one minister depart, leaving behind two policy papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cabinet' suggests government ministers, but here it is a piece of furniture; lose its last letter. 'Leaving' means bequeathing, not departing.
explanation.definitionFit: John Locke, the English philosopher, wrote the Two Treatises of Government, published in 1689.

clue.text: Top sin to get Dante’s Cocytus?

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: a vice is a sin or moral failing

explanation.surface: Asking whether the worst sin earns a place in the lowest pit of Dante's Hell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top sin' reads as the gravest sin, but 'Top' is a verb meaning behead. In Dante's Inferno, Cocytus is the frozen lake at the bottom of Hell where traitors are trapped.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocytus in the Inferno is a lake frozen solid, so the question mark marks a definition by example.

clue.text: Lead function set up by a university for those like Napoleon

indicators.note: in a down entry, setting something up raises it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
U is the standard abbreviation for university
the star of a show plays the lead
cot is the cotangent, a trigonometric function

explanation.surface: A university appointing someone to a leading role, aimed at aspiring Napoleons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' could be the metal, but it is the starring role; the mathematical function cot is easily missed. The reversed pair comes after A and U.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon ruled France with absolute personal power, the defining trait of a dictatorial ruler.

clue.text: Old city dictator’s flag

indicators.note: a dictator here is one who dictates, speaking words for someone to write down, so what follows is a sound

blocks.note: to flag is to tire or weaken

explanation.surface: Names an ancient city and the banner flown by its tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' summons a tyrant, which is tempting with these letters, but it means a person dictating aloud. 'Flag' is the verb, not a banner.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyre was an ancient Phoenician port, now in southern Lebanon, famed for purple dye.

clue.text: One that lighted fools when the rest weren’t born?

definitions.text: One that lighted fools when the rest weren’t born?

blocks.note: surface reading: some lamp or lantern-bearer that lit the way for foolish people
setter's reading: Macbeth says past days have lit fools the way to dusty death, and the days still to come have not yet arrived

explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Macbeth's 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow' speech: 'all our yesterdays have lighted fools the way to dusty death'. Only past days exist; the rest are still unborn.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's line makes past days the things that light fools' way, and future days have not come into being.

clue.text: English crime writer finally promoted? She’s trying!

indicators.note: being promoted means moving up, and in a down entry the final letter rises to the top of its word

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English
Dorothy L. Sayers wrote the Lord Peter Wimsey detective novels

explanation.surface: Wondering whether an English crime novelist won promotion, with an exasperated remark about her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She's trying' sounds like 'she's tiresome', but means she is making an attempt. Move the writer's last letter to her front, then put E before.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay is to attempt or try, so an essayer is one who makes an attempt.

clue.text: Fraulein Bunt‘s pilot, stripped of his wings

indicators.note: a word's wings are its two ends, so stripping them off removes the outer letters

blocks.note: an airman is a pilot

explanation.surface: A German woman's pilot has been grounded, losing his flying badge.
explanation.walkthrough: Irma Bunt is Blofeld's henchwoman in Ian Fleming's Bond novels. 'Wings' suggests a pilot's badge, but it means the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fraulein Irma Bunt appears in On Her Majesty's Secret Service, so her given name is wanted.

clue.text: Lib-Dem rows about censorship

indicators.note: to bring something about is to turn it round, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of the party name and the quarrels, taken together

explanation.surface: Liberal Democrat party quarrels over freedom of expression.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lib Dems are Britain's Liberal Democrat party. Thomas Bowdler published an expurgated Family Shakespeare, giving his name to prudish cutting of texts.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowdlerism is the practice of removing passages thought improper from books, a form of literary expurgation.

clue.text: He kept Pilot men circling a city

indicators.note: circling means going round, so the word turns back on itself

blocks.note: OR, other ranks, means ordinary soldiers
Chester is a cathedral city in Cheshire, England

explanation.surface: Someone retained a ship's pilot while the crew went round a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pilot' looks like a navigator, but it is Mr Rochester's dog in Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Rochester owns the big dog named Pilot that Jane first meets on the icy lane near Thornfield.

clue.text: One is where the Alchemist’s found oxygen unmodified

definitions.text: One is where the Alchemist’s found

blocks.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
'as is' means unchanged, without modification

explanation.surface: An alchemist in his laboratory discovers oxygen in its pure, unaltered state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alchemist' and 'oxygen' suggest a laboratory, but this is Paulo Coelho's novel The Alchemist, in which the boy Santiago meets the alchemist at a desert stopping place.
explanation.definitionFit: In Coelho's novel the alchemist lives at the Al-Fayoum desert settlement, so such a watered spot is where he is found.

clue.text: He tried to force a union, for example, then another succeeded

definitions.text: He tried to force a union

blocks.note: e.g. abbreviates exempli gratia, for example
another union, the European Union, abbreviated EU
S is the abbreviation for succeeded in family trees

explanation.surface: One attempt at a merger is cited, and then a second attempt worked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' refers back to 'a union' in the definition: a second union, the EU. Egeus, in A Midsummer Night's Dream, demands that his daughter Hermia marry Demetrius.
explanation.definitionFit: Hermia's father insists on her wedding Demetrius against her wishes, invoking Athenian law to compel it.

clue.text: One applying to watch birds will do just that

definitions.text: One applying to watch birds will do just that

blocks.note: surface reading: an applicant for a birdwatching job
setter's reading: swap the opening sounds of 'watch birds' and you get 'botch words', which is exactly what this slip of the tongue does

explanation.walkthrough: Exchanging the initial sounds of 'watch birds' gives 'botch words'. The device named after Rev. William Spooner applied to the phrase does just what it produces.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford don Spooner was famous for transposing the initial sounds of words, so his eponymous slip garbles speech.

clue.text: Where to keep wicked things like Philip Marlowe books?

blocks.note: first meaning: a store for candles, which have wicks
second meaning: in the style of Raymond Chandler, who created the detective Marlowe

explanation.surface: Asking where to shelve sinful items such as hard-boiled detective fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked' means having a wick, not evil. The second meaning invents an adjective from the novelist's surname plus -Y.
explanation.definitionFit: A chandlery is a candle store; whimsically, Chandler-y describes writing resembling Raymond Chandler's crime novels.

clue.text: Opera House opera losing millions

indicators.note: to lose something is to be without it, so a letter drops out

blocks.note: Leo is one of the twelve houses, or signs, of the zodiac
Norma is Bellini's opera
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: An opera house drops a production because it costs too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opera House' reads as one venue, but it splits: the first word is the definition and House is a zodiac sign. Take M from Bellini's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonora was the first version of Beethoven's Fidelio and the title of William Henry Fry's American opera.

clue.text: Means to test a solution assembled amid Romeo’s raving

indicators.note: to be amid something is to sit in its middle, so one piece goes inside another
raving means wild and deranged, so these letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the name and its possessive S
people who met have gathered or assembled

explanation.surface: A lovesick Romeo raves while someone puts together a way to check an answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solution' means a liquid mixture, not an answer. The jumbled letters of ROMEOS surround MET.
explanation.definitionFit: An osmometer measures the osmotic pressure of a chemical solution, so it is an instrument for testing one.

clue.text: At last book dealer ordered Shirley

indicators.note: at last points to the end, so only the final letter is kept
ordered means put into a new arrangement, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the closing letter of this word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bookseller finally placed an order for a customer named Shirley.
explanation.walkthrough: Shirley looks like a customer's first name; it is the title of Charlotte Brontë's novel, whose heroine is the heiress Shirley Keeldar.
explanation.definitionFit: Brontë's 1849 novel takes its title from its heroine's first name, so her surname is a fair answer.

clue.text: Slept around and turned up in a novel

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning something up flips it to read upward
a word going around another surrounds it

blocks.note: to kip is British slang for to sleep
taken as written

explanation.surface: A promiscuous character who later turned up in fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slept around' looks like one idiom for promiscuity, but 'around' is the container signal and 'and' is fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson's 1886 adventure story follows David Balfour, seized and shipped off against his will.

clue.text: I’m thinking this writer’s against small animals

blocks.note: er is the sound of someone hesitating while thinking
what belongs to this writer is mine, with the possessive S kept

explanation.surface: An author hesitantly declares opposition to little creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter speaking of themself, so 'this writer's' is 'mine's'. 'Against' just sets the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Ermine is the stoat in its white winter coat, a small carnivorous mammal of the weasel family.

clue.text: Write as Gray did, say, plugging a subject of Beethoven’s

indicators.note: a plug fills a hole, so one piece is pushed inside the other

blocks.note: Beethoven's piano piece Für Elise is addressed to Elise
say means for example, e.g.

explanation.surface: Writing in the manner of Gray while promoting a Beethoven work.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray wrote Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard. 'Say' is not speech but the example abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To elegise is to compose a mournful poem, as Gray famously did in his churchyard lament.

clue.text: She had Diomedes twirling, see, like a piper!

indicators.note: twirling means spinning round, so the letters turn back to front

blocks.note: a see is a bishop's diocese; Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
the Pied Piper of Hamelin wore multicoloured clothes

explanation.surface: A woman sets the hero Diomedes spinning like a dancing piper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twirling' suggests dancing, but it turns the whole joined phrase round. 'Had' means gave birth to.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Deipyle, wife of Tydeus, bore the hero Diomedes, who fought at Troy.

clue.text: Lacking sex, topless exercise gives inspiration to musicians

indicators.note: in a down entry, the top is the first letter, so going without it drops that letter

blocks.note: neuter means having no sex
PE is physical education, school exercise

explanation.surface: Celibate, half-dressed workouts are said to inspire musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' seems to describe the exercise but beheads the sexless word. The pieces read as a racy headline.
explanation.definitionFit: Euterpe is the Greek Muse of music and lyric poetry, so she inspires those who play.

clue.text: Originally set in stone by a girl claiming sanctuary

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the first letter counts
a piece put in another sits inside it

blocks.note: an emerald is a precious green stone
the opening letter of this word
taken as written

explanation.surface: An inscription carved in stone by a young woman seeking refuge.
explanation.walkthrough: In Victor Hugo's The Hunchback of Notre-Dame, Quasimodo carries Esmeralda into the cathedral, crying 'Sanctuary!'
explanation.definitionFit: Hugo's gypsy heroine is given refuge inside Notre-Dame from those condemning her to hang.

clue.text: Not all Apollo tells about his mother

indicators.note: not all of the words is used, only a stretch lying within them
about means turned round, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a run of letters crossing the two words

explanation.surface: Apollo keeps some things back when he talks about his mother.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is fitting since the answer is truly Apollo's mother, and its letters lie backwards in his own name and words.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Titaness Leto bore the twins Apollo and Artemis to Zeus on Delos.

clue.text: Get up on stage

blocks.note: first meaning: climb on, as onto a horse
second meaning: put on a production or event

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an actor climbing onto the boards, but 'stage' is a verb meaning to put on a show.
explanation.definitionFit: One can climb onto a horse, and a company can present a play or an exhibition, both with this verb.

clue.text: Relative success for JP Martin

blocks.note: first meaning: a parent's brother
second meaning: the title of J. P. Martin's best-known children's book, about a wealthy elephant

explanation.walkthrough: 'Relative success' suggests moderate achievement, but the words split: J. P. Martin's Uncle books, about a rich elephant, were his hit.
explanation.definitionFit: A parent's brother is a family member, and Martin's 1964 book of that title was his celebrated work.

clue.text: Stroke part of poet’s foot

blocks.note: first meaning: in medicine, a seizure or sudden attack
second meaning: the stressed beat in a metrical foot

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a poet's injured foot, but a foot here is a unit of metre.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word means a blow; in medicine it is a seizure and in prosody the stressed syllable of a foot.

clue.text: Shift carpet and he can perform

indicators.note: to shift is to move things about, so these letters change places

blocks.note: the two words taken as written

explanation.surface: Roll back the rug and he can do his act.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: a tap routine needs a hard floor, so the rug must be moved before he can perform.
explanation.definitionFit: A tap routine is a stage act, so the performer is someone who can put on a show with his shoes.

clue.text: End in sight

blocks.note: first meaning: a goal or purpose
second meaning: as a verb, to sight or point a weapon at a target

explanation.walkthrough: 'End in sight' is a stock phrase for an approaching finish; split it, with 'in' as the join.
explanation.definitionFit: An end is a purpose or goal, and to sight a gun is to point it at a target.

clue.text: Pound a book!

blocks.note: first meaning: the first name of the American modernist poet Pound
second meaning: a book of the Old Testament

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as an order to thump a volume, but Pound is the American modernist poet, identified by his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The modernist poet's first name doubles as the title of a book of the Hebrew Bible.

clue.text: A novel plot pinched by Agatha Christie, perhaps

indicators.note: something pinched is gripped tightly, so one piece is squeezed inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
Agatha Christie was made a Dame, a title for a woman given a knighthood-level honour
a plot of ground, as in a flower bed

explanation.surface: Agatha Christie is accused of stealing the plot of a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' suggests a storyline, apt for Christie, but it is a garden plot. 'A novel' tempts as the whole definition; the A is part of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Bede was George Eliot's first full-length work of fiction, published in 1859.
